Sustainability Spotlight · Fashion

Can luxury fashion become circular?

What Marine Serre's Partnerships Reveal

French label Marine Serre turns discarded textiles into luxury clothing. But can partnerships alone make fashion circular?

00 · Introduction

Fashionhas a wasteproblem.

Fashion has a waste problem. The industry still relies heavily on a linear model: extract resources, make garments, sell them and eventually throw them away. The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP, 2025) reports that approximately 92 million tonnes of textile waste are generated globally each year. In 2023, only 8% of textile fibres came from recycled sources.

French label Marine Serre has built its identity around an alternative: upcycling. But can circular luxury succeed through one brand’s creativity, or does it depend on its partners? Using the Relational View, this article argues that Marine Serre illustrates how supply chain relationships can help turn discarded textiles into commercial value. However, limited transparency and questions about scalability make it difficult to assess how far its sustainability model can go.

Upcycling: existing materials, new garmentsLê Bảo Vy
01 · The linear model

The problem withlinear fashion

92Mt

The damage goes beyond landfill. Fibre production, dyeing and manufacturing consume water and energy, while chemical pollution and emissions occur throughout the fashion value chain (Niinimäki et al., 2020). Recycling more clothes cannot solve this problem alone. A circular economy aims to keep materials and products in use for longer.

Upcycling is one approach: it transforms existing materials or discarded products into new items rather than simply processing them back into raw fibres (Aus et al., 2021).

02 · The brand

MarineSerre'sapproach

Marine Serre states that regenerating garments has been central to its design philosophy since its debut collection in 2016. The brand uses deadstock fabrics, end-of-life materials and existing garments to create new products (Marine Serre, n.d.-b).

According to its sustainability page, upcycled materials are sourced in Europe, sorted, washed and treated at the brand’s Paris headquarters before being sent to European manufacturing partners.

For its Fall–Winter 2025 show, Marine Serre reports that 50% of the products presented were upcycled, while the remaining 50% used certified and recycled fibres (Marine Serre, n.d.-a). Its values page also identifies long-standing collaborations with factories in Italy, Portugal and France.

50%of fabric leftovers could be turned into new garments (Aus et al., 2021)

Upcycling is more complicated than simply replacing new fabric with old fabric. A five-year practice-led study across four garment factories found that fabric leftovers accounted for 25–40% of the material used in production. The researchers also found that up to 50% of these leftovers could be turned into new garments (Aus et al., 2021). However, upcycled designs must respond to the size, quality and availability of existing materials. This makes coordination between designers and manufacturers important.

03 · Theory

Whypartnershipsmatter

The Relational View

Dyer and Singh (1998) argue that competitive advantage can emerge from relationships between businesses, not only from resources owned by individual firms. Their Relational View identifies four sources of relational advantage: relation-specific assets, knowledge-sharing routines, complementary resources and capabilities, and effective governance. Marine Serre’s public information provides different levels of evidence for each.

01

Complementary resources and capabilities

Clearest example
Public evidenceStrong

Complementary resources and capabilities are the clearest example. Marine Serre contributes its design direction and approach to material regeneration, while its European manufacturing partners provide the production capabilities needed to turn those materials into finished garments. These contributions can create value that neither party could achieve as effectively alone. In a study of seven Italian textile companies, Colombo et al. (2025) found that complementary resources supported circular practices in six cases.

02

Knowledge-sharing routines

Less clearly documented
Public evidencePartial

Knowledge-sharing routines are less clearly documented. Upcycling requires designers and manufacturers to exchange information about material quality, construction techniques and production limitations. Colombo et al. (2025) identify knowledge-sharing as the most important relational enabler for circular practices in their study. Marine Serre publishes films showing its production locations and artisans, but its public information provides limited detail about how technical knowledge is shared with manufacturing partners. The potential benefit is clear, but the actual process remains difficult to assess.

03

Relation-specific assets

Difficult to verify
Public evidenceLimited

Relation-specific assets are also difficult to verify. These are investments made by partners specifically for a particular relationship, such as customised equipment or dedicated expertise (Dyer & Singh, 1998). Marine Serre’s Paris-based sorting and treatment process demonstrates investment in its own operations, but public information does not establish whether its manufacturing partners make comparable relationship-specific investments. Colombo et al. (2025) found that this was the least influential relational enabler in their textile industry cases, although it was still present in six of the seven companies studied.

04

Effective governance

Evidence is limited
Public evidenceLimited

Effective governance is another area where evidence is limited. Marine Serre states that each regenerated garment carries a label identifying its material, origin and place of transformation (Marine Serre, n.d.-b). This improves product-level traceability, but it does not demonstrate how the brand and its manufacturing partners coordinate responsibilities, share risks or monitor sustainability performance. Colombo et al. (2025) emphasise that transparency and aligned goals are important conditions for successful circular partnerships. Similarly, Mahanty and Domenech (2024) found that fragmented knowledge and different understandings of circularity can prevent stakeholders across the fashion value chain from working towards shared objectives.

Bars show how strongly Marine Serre's public information supports each source of relational advantage, as assessed in this article.

04 · Critical view

The limits ofcircular luxury

Scale?
01

Scalability

Scalability: Upcycling has potential, but expanding it is not straightforward. Existing materials vary in quantity, quality, colour and condition, making production planning more difficult than using standardised new fabrics. Aus et al. (2021) found that industrial upcycling requires better visibility of available waste and designs adapted to the materials. Marine Serre also acknowledges that each upcycled item may differ in shade or print depending on the material used (Marine Serre, n.d.-a). This uniqueness supports the brand's identity, but may complicate consistent large-scale production.

02

Environmental proof

Environmental proof: Reusing materials does not automatically guarantee a lower environmental impact. Sorting, washing, treatment and transportation also consume resources. Rehman et al. (2024) demonstrate how waste-flow mapping and Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) can help measure environmental impacts across fashion supply chains. However, the public sources reviewed for this article do not provide independently verified lifecycle data quantifying the environmental savings of Marine Serre's overall production model.

03

Self-reported evidence

Self-reported evidence: Much of the available information about Marine Serre's sourcing and production practices comes from the brand itself. These disclosures provide useful insight, but they are not the same as independent verification. To strengthen its sustainability claims, the brand could publish independently assessed lifecycle data, disclose more about how partners share knowledge and investment, and establish measurable waste-diversion targets.

05 · Global goals

Linking circular fashionto the SustainableDevelopment Goals

12
Strongest connection

SDG 12: Responsible Consumption and Production is the strongest connection. Reusing existing materials and extending their value can support more responsible resource use and waste reduction (United Nations, n.d.-a).

13
Also relevant

SDG 13: Climate Action is also relevant because reducing reliance on newly produced materials may help lower emissions. However, lifecycle data is needed to demonstrate the actual impact (United Nations, n.d.-b).

17
Cooperation

SDG 17: Partnerships for the Goals highlights the importance of cooperation. Marine Serre's relationships with manufacturing partners illustrate supply chain collaboration, although SDG 17 also calls for broader partnerships involving governments, businesses and other stakeholders (United Nations, n.d.-c).

06 · Conclusion

Conclusion

Marine Serre shows how luxury fashion can create value from materials that might otherwise go unused. Through the Relational View, its relationships with manufacturing partners can be understood as strategic resources that support circular production. However, partnerships alone do not guarantee sustainability. Their effectiveness depends on knowledge-sharing, transparency, aligned goals and measurable environmental outcomes. Ultimately, circular luxury will depend not only on what brands create, but also on how effectively their supply chain partners work together.

Partnerships alone do not guarantee sustainability.
